quote: it may take the form of interjections like English Damn!
note: Also p. 74 ("exclamations like Fuck!, Shit! Damn!, Bugger!, Bloody hell!, Fucking hell!") and p. 83 ("developed into a formula exactly parallel to single-word interjections like Damn!, Fuck! and Shit!")

quote: in supplements like . . . Damn, we’ve missed the bus again . . . are best regarded as having been reanalysed as interjections.
note: Secondary: Ljung is quoting Huddleston & Pullum 2002: 1361

quote: REACT: Reactive interjection, GF: gap filler, BC: before clause
note: Table 4.5, Damn row: REACT 0, GF 1 (25%), BC 2 (50%), BW 1 (25%), total 4. A gap filler is a complete turn. Note 4 (p. 171, "DAMN: Damn it 2, Damn 2 = 4") shows half the tokens are *Damn it*, so the DAMN_REACT/DAMN_NP split is unknown. Zero reactive tokens. Ljung warns that low-N rows are "rather uninteresting" (p. 93)

quote: the most common position is before a clause over which they have scope.
note: Table 4.5 gives Damn 2 "before clause" slot-filler tokens. This is the supplement-like position. The same *Damn it* caveat applies

quote: DAMN: Damn it 2, Damn 2 = 4
note: Table 4.3 (p. 81): Damn single 2 (50%), combined 2 (50%). The combinations are all *Damn it*

quote: despite the clearly different literal meanings of fuck, damn and sod, these words are freely
note: The sentence continues across a hyphen break: "...interchangeable in curses like Fuck you!, Damn you! and Sod you! and in interjections like Fuck!, Damn! and Sod it!"

quote: All that has happened is that Oh damn it! has changed roles.
note: (25) *Oh damn it.* starts as a reactive interjection and becomes the first turn once the hearer replies *What?*. The form *damn it* can't be assigned to one use

quote: exclamations of irritation, pain or surprise containing expletives
note: Members named include Damn! (DAMN_REACT), Fuck!, Shit!, Bugger!, Bloody hell!, God!, Gosh!, Crikey!

quote: Interjections generally express surprise, pain, fear, anger,
note: Continues "disappointment and even joy". Members: God!, Shit!, Fuck!, Damn!, Hell!, Bloody hell!

quote: reactive interjections do not have meanings in the established sense of the term.
note: Examples: Oh my god, Shit!, Oh bloody hell! Damn has no reactive tokens in Table 4.5

quote: they have little or no propositional meaning
note: Ljung applies Brinton's (1996) pragmatic-marker criteria. Per Table 4.5, all 4 Damn tokens are in this class

quote: It appears that the non-reactive expletive interjections meet all of these criteria
note: One of those criteria is Brinton's (6): "occur either outside the syntactic structure or are attached to it". The usual position is before a clause (p. 87). Examples: Cor that was a proper macho man!; bloody hell look at that old codger

quote: do not combine with other words in integrated syntactic constructions, and have expressive rather than propositional meaning
note: Secondary source. Also supports P07 Y. Central members named: ah, hey, oops, ouch, sh, wow

quote: used as expressive exclamations, on their own, or as supplements with clausal anchors
note: Secondary source. Members as in the row above

quote: positive or negative emotional reactions to what is being or has just been said or to something in the situation
note: Secondary (Carter & McCarthy 2006: 224). Members named include damn, heavens, ouch, ugh, wow. **This is the only mention of HEAVENS in the book**

quote: deviant forms some of which exhibit peculiarities in the relation between spelling and pronunciation, for instance tsktsk, tut-tut, sh and ugh
note: Ljung reporting Quirk et al. 1985 §2.58 Note ("quasi-linguistic noises"). No phonetic forms are given. For TUTTUT, the brief excludes the spelling pronunciation

quote: forms like Ah!, Aha!, Mm!, Oh!, Ouch! and Wow!
note: Preceded on p. 76 by "the class as such also includes phonologically regular". Reported from Quirk et al. No forms are transcribed, so this may fall short of P13's "given in full" negative standard

quote: the examples Crikey!, gee! and gosh! have no homonyms
note: Gehweiler 2008 as reported. Figure 4.1 (p. 80) puts Gee! among the primary (−homonym) "moderated expletives". p. 78: gee evolved via Jesus!

quote: Outside of the interjectional context, God and Jesus may never be replaced by Gosh and Gee
note: Starred example: *Gee died on the cross. This shows gee has no argument (noun) use. It doesn't restrict the interjection use itself

item_id: CLASS:WH-emphasizers (the hell, the heck, the devil, the fuck)
quote: are used as pure emphasizers after interrogative WH-words
note: THE_HELL_WH is a member. "Pure emphasizers": no named feeling is assigned, so no P08 claim

quote: The function of hell in who the hell is clearly just emphatic and the word can be replaced with the Devil, the fuck, etc.
note: Who the hell... counts as swearing (no literal or metaphorical meaning left)

quote: In such constructions the taboo words may be replaced by the prepositional phrases like on earth, in the whole world, in God’s name, in the name of God
note: The non-taboo substitutes are PPs. *exactly* is never mentioned

quote: Where the fuck/the hell/the Devil/ did you put it?
note: Exemplified inside the interrogative clause. Ljung calls it an emphasizer in the "emphatic slot", never a modifier

quote: placing certain swear words immediately after an interrogative pronoun or adverb
note: Listed under the emphasis function of slot fillers

quote: involve placing a ‘swear word’ in the right slot in a given string, as for instance in What the hell do you mean? and absobloodylutely.
note: This is the basis for the class P01 N row below

quote: resist semantic and syntactic analysis and have to be learnt as wholes.
note: The example is What the fuck do you mean?. Same page: "Anomalous syntax/usage is also common in swearing" (what/where/who the devil/fuck, absofuckinglutely, Henry the bloody Eighth)

quote: A very common slot-filler function is that of intensifier expressing a high degree of the following adjective or adverb
note: Examples on the same page: It's bloody marvellous; They drove damn fast. These are the glosses' own examples

quote: (1) as degree adverbs, for instance in bloody impressive, goddamn quickly

In (1) and (3) the degree adverbs damn and bloody indicate a high degree of the following adverbs well and quickly, and in (2) and (4) the same degree adverbs modify the adjectives sure and hard in the same way.
note: damn well, bloody quickly, damn sure, bloody hard work

quote: The adverbs considered here obviously belong to the first category, that is, they are amplifiers
note: Quirk's amplifier/downtoner split

quote: they function in the same way as very, highly or extremely, with the difference that these three words lack the taboo load
note: Same function as *very*; taboo load is the only difference stated

quote: they function in the same way as very, highly or extremely, with the difference that these three words lack the taboo load
note: Control

quote: From a grammatical point of view, there is no difference between the two examples above and examples like He’s so very lazy
note: The two examples are He's so fucking/bloody/goddamned lazy and The fucking/bloody/goddamned postman hasn't been yet (vs The useless/no-good postman). Ljung exempts these uses from formulaicity

quote: they are modifiers, viz. their scope is local, extending no further than the nearest element to the right.
note: Members: BLOODY_INTENS, DAMN_DEGREE, and the intensifying-adjective tokens of BLOODY_PRENOM/DAMN_PRENOM

quote: they have clearly defined meanings
note: My judgement call. Ljung assigns a high-degree meaning parallel to *very* and contrasts it with the hard-to-specify non-intensifying uses. He never says "truth-conditional". Code U if P07's N standard needs explicit descriptive content

quote: as an intensifier of adverbs than of adjectives, while damn does not show similar tendencies towards specialization.
note: Ch. 7 note 5. The same note says degree *bloody* is "much less common" with adverbs, so BLOODY_INTENS = Y (prefers adjectives)

quote: intensifiers or adjectives of dislike as in English She is damn(ed) clever! and The damn(ed) car wouldn’t start!
note: *damn(ed) clever* is DAMN_DEGREE

quote: intensifiers or adjectives of dislike as in English She is damn(ed) clever! and The damn(ed) car wouldn’t start!
note: *The damn(ed) car* is an "adjective of dislike"

item_id: damn(ed) [use not in the 46; nearest DAMN_DEGREE]
quote: both bloody and fucking are found as emphasizers before all sorts of clause constituents. Note that it is impossible to use damn(ed) in such a way.
note: bloody and fucking = Y: I wish they'd all bloody leave me alone; You fucking stink; We're always fucking late. Parallels CGEL's *I damn hated it

quote: A strong case can be made for including bloody, damn and their equivalents among the intensifying adjectives when they are used to indicate degree with regard to a following gradable noun
note: Examples: Bye you damn fools; You bloody idiot!; a bloody nightmare; too much damn pain. p. 33 has It's a bloody miracle

quote: Obviously there is also an element of dislike however.
note: Said of the intensifying-adjective tokens

quote: DISLIKE constructions in which bloody, damn, etc. serve to express the speaker’s dislike of the referent(s) of a following noun
note: Examples: That damn Paul... (before a proper noun); (10) Damn heater!; that bloody pencil sharpener thing. *Damn heater!* is classed as adjective + noun, not as a curse. Ljung gives no criterion separating it from DAMN_NP

quote: as adjectives of dislike as in I can’t stand that bloody cashier.
Another slot-filler function for swear words is to indicate that the speaker dislikes the referent of the following noun.
note: bloody is the named member

quote: using alternately bloody, fucking, damned, goddamned, flipping to express negative attitude or simply emphasis
note: Example: I can't open the damned/fucking/bloody... door. The form here is *damned*, not *damn*. "or simply emphasis" makes stance optional

quote: the use of fucking, bloody, goddamned, etc. as intensifiers and as adjectival attributes
note: Example: The fucking/bloody/goddamned postman hasn't been yet

quote: There are also cases which undoubtedly express dislike on the part of the speaker, but whose main function seems to be to place emphasis on a certain noun
note: Examples: in the bloody book; go to a damn doctor; (p. 150) the fucking underwear department; (p. 34) not a bloody bathtub

quote: In (14) there may be an additional element of dislike but not in (15).
note: (15) is *in the fucking underwear department*. Ljung excludes dislike for this token only; the same page says emphasis plus dislike seems "to be the rule rather than the exception". Treat as mixed evidence

quote: fucking which serves both as emphatic and/or derogatory adjective and as adverb of degree
By placing damn and bloody immediately after worst, every, 30 and no, the speaker emphasizes these elements, which are also no doubt pronounced with heavy stress.
note: Examples: the worst damn place; Every damn call; 30 damn years; no bloody money. The stress claim concerns the preceding word, so it isn't P12

quote: these words often occur in what looks like typical NP modifier positions and that when they are used in this position it is difficult to free oneself from the impulse to regard them as modifiers
note: Example: It's not her bloody husband ≈ He's not her husband, for God's sake. This is a warning against reading P03 off position

quote: the speaker actually creates a kind of epithet NP by including bloody before a normally non-epithet noun
note: Example: You bloody/stupid teacher(s)!. bloody is grouped with *stupid* as "disparaging or negative adjectives"

quote: Heavy stress on book and doctor would have supported the second interpretation.
note: Stress on the following noun would favour emphasis over dislike. Ljung couldn't check (no phonological annotation in BNC). Not P12

item_id: CLASS:expletive slot fillers (bloody, damn, damned, goddamn(ed), fucking)
quote: By definition, the expletive slot fillers are all used inside larger units.
note: Also "swear words that are not themselves independent utterances" (p. 143). Caution: ch. 4 also calls clause-initial interjections "slot fillers" (p. 87), and *Bloody fool!* / *Damn heater!* place these words inside standalone NPs

quote: they are intended as swearing: their meanings are taboo, they are not used with their literal meanings
note: bloody, damn(d), fucking. Under 1% of BNC *bloody* tokens are literal "blood-stained" (p. 144)

item_id: CLASS:slot fillers inside NPs and words
quote: the main – or perhaps even the only – function of the swearing expressions is to express the speaker’s attitudes and feelings.
note: Members: Henry the bloody Eighth, absofuckinglutely, kanga-bloodyroo (BLOODY_INFIX)

quote: Emphasis may also take the form of infixation in a word as in Absobloodylutely, Infuckingcredible, Kangabloodyroo
note: Phrase-level insertion also listed: Henry the fucking Eighth

quote: insertion of the expletive element into linguistic units normally considered to be impenetrable, viz. words and phrases
note: Applies to "certain but not all" emphasizers. Examples mix phrase-level (into bloody perspective, at bloody home, Abu bleeding Dabi) and word-level (Unfuckingconscious). Table 7.2 (p. 155): bloody insertion 26/318, fucking 8/191; both levels counted together

item_id: infixed fucking (use not in the 46; bears on BLOODY_INFIX)
quote: uses of fuck that can no longer be accounted for in terms of traditional word classes, as when it is used ‘intrusively’
note: Said of fucking, not bloody

quote: (10) You bastard/son of a bitch/dickhead!/Bastard!/Son of a bitch!
note: Direct-address name-calling. Bare *Bastard!* is also given

quote: exclamations with or without an initial You used to express the speaker’s negative attitude towards the addressee.
note: Members: traitor, idiot, snob, bastard, son of a bitch, dickhead

quote: By testing different nouns in such utterances we can conclude that the nouns traitor, idiot and snob, for example, are all epithets
note: *You teacher! fails (p. 127); bastard passes (p. 128). Ljung's own epithet diagnostic

quote: The nouns used in these constructions are all evaluative: they are used to express the speaker’s – negative or positive – opinion of
present-day uses/meanings of the words which are non-denotative and merely express the speaker’s negative opinion
note: Table 6.3 members include bastard ("Contemptible person 16C+"; "Man, person, fellow 1910s UK")

quote: it must have taboo meaning, it must have non-literal meaning which is not metaphorically linked to its literal meaning, and it must be able to appear in all three types of name-calling
note: bastard qualifies (pp. 125, 128)

quote: The standard insults, the unfriendly suggestions and name-calling express the speaker’s feelings towards the addressee at the moment of speech.
note: Contrasted with curses, which wish evil in the future. Ljung's wording, not Potts's terms

quote: the exclamation The fool/idiot! must be a response to information provided by an interlocutor.
note: Example (11), p. 128: John refuses to pay for the meal. – The bastard/son of a bitch!. It is a separate response turn, so it gives **no P02 evidence**; the supplement use itself is never exemplified

quote: where Damn, Fuck and Sod are examples of optative subjunctives of the same kind as live in Long live the Queen!
note: Example: Damn you!. Ch. 5 note 3 (p. 172): "the ‘simple verb form’ lacks agreement with third person subjects and is in fact a subjunctive". Relevant to P05 opportunities; not an invariance claim

quote: curses like Damn you!, Damn this place! with the basic meanings ‘May you/this place be damned!’
note: p. 55: "the word God is understood"

quote: (21) . . . they’re not doing a bad job, damn them. (BNC KGX 139)
note: The curse follows a complete clause

quote: expressing the speaker’s dislike of something or somebody and meeting the requirements that neither God nor the Devil are used referentially
note: Members: the devil take…, God damn America, damn them (DAMN_NP), Fucking fuck the pair of you!

quote: (21) Damn paint and stuff, cor strewth. (KBR 531)
note: Ljung: "exclaims Damn paint and stuff!" (pp. 89–90). Could be curse + NP, or dislike adjective + noun like *Damn heater!*. I can't tell which

quote: what we can do, more or less adequately, is to describe the range of ‘meanings’ that may be assigned to such
note: p. 23: "even the speakers themselves may be uncertain about the exact nature of the feelings that triggered their use of swearing." Ljung's claim is that the particular feeling is underdetermined, which is not quite Potts's ineffability

quote: aims a direct expression of the speaker’s attitude toward what he is speaking about
note: Jakobson, quoted. The attitude is anchored to the speaker; Ljung never discusses any other perspective
